opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important shift is that the environment is no longer just a place where you evaluate the model. It's where the model learns. When we train agents with reinforcement learning, the environment becomes part of the training data. So the quality, diversity, and realism of environments directly shape what capabilities emerge.

When designing tools, my first principle is to keep them general rather than hand-crafted for one narrow task. If you build a very specialized tool for every scenario, the model learns to depend on that scaffolding, and it doesn't generalize. But if you give it a small set of powerful, composable primitives, like search, a code interpreter, a browser, a file system, then the model has to learn how to combine them. That kind of compositional skill transfers much better.

The second principle is verifiability. For RL to work, you need a reward signal you can trust. Coding and math are popular partly because you can check the answer. For more open-ended agentic tasks, like research or multi-step workflows, a lot of the real work is designing environments where success can be judged reliably, whether through test cases, structured outcomes, or a strong model acting as a judge, without the agent being able to hack the reward.

Third, the environment has to feel like the real world, including its messiness. Real web pages are noisy, tools fail, APIs return errors, information conflicts. If you train only in clean sandboxes, the agent becomes brittle the moment it meets reality. So we deliberately want long horizons, partial information, and the need to recover from mistakes. Long-horizon ability, staying coherent over dozens or hundreds of steps, is one of the key frontiers now.

And finally, scale. One environment, however well designed, isn't enough. You want a very large number of diverse tasks so the model learns underlying skills rather than memorizing patterns. In some sense, building environments is becoming like building pretraining data was a few years ago. It's the new bottleneck, and the teams that figure out how to scale high-quality environments will have a real advantage.

So my overall view is: give the model general tools, put it in realistic and verifiable environments, and let it learn through interaction. Don't over-engineer the workflow for it. The less we hard-code human assumptions, the more room the model has to discover better strategies on its own.

r001.rationale: The response discusses general principles for designing agent tools and training environments, but it does not distinguish adapting environments to a given model from proactively designing them while building a first-party product.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key shift is that we should stop thinking about tools as things we hand to a model, and start thinking about the environment as the thing that actually shapes the model.

When people say "designing tools for agents," there's usually an implicit assumption that the model is fixed and you're just giving it more capabilities, like a bigger toolbox. But if you're training the model with reinforcement learning, the environment is the training signal. The tools you expose, the feedback the agent gets, the latency, the error messages, the way failures show up, all of that gets baked into the model's behavior. So environment design is really a form of model design.

A few things I've come to believe.

First, the environment should be as close to the real world as possible, but it also has to be verifiable. Those two things pull against each other. The real world is messy and the reward is ambiguous. A toy environment is clean but the model learns the toy. The hard engineering work is finding tasks where the outcome is actually checkable, like code that runs, a search result that's correct, a file that ends up in the right state, while keeping enough of the real messiness that the skills transfer. Coding has been a good starting point precisely because it sits in that intersection, but I don't think it's the end point.

Second, the tool interface matters more than people expect. If a tool returns a wall of unstructured text, the model wastes its context and attention parsing it. If a tool fails silently, the model never learns to recover. We spent a lot of time on things that sound boring, like what an error looks like, how much of a long output to return, whether the agent can see intermediate state. Those details decide whether the model learns good long-horizon behavior or learns to hallucinate around gaps.

Third, I think the number of tools is a distraction. There's a temptation to expose hundreds of APIs and call it an agent platform. In practice a small set of general tools, like executing code, searching, reading and writing files, covers a very large fraction of tasks, because the model can compose them. A model that can write and run code effectively has access to every library that exists. So I'd rather invest in making a few primitives very robust than in integrating many shallow ones.

And then there's the scaling question, which is really about diversity. For pretraining, scale came from text on the internet. For agents, the equivalent is a large and diverse distribution of environments and tasks. Nobody has that yet. Building it is partly data work, partly infrastructure, and partly a kind of taste about what tasks actually make the model smarter rather than just better at one benchmark. I think over the next couple of years that's going to be one of the main sources of differentiation between labs, more than architecture.

So to answer directly: I think of environment design as the new data curation. The question is not "what tools does the agent have," it's "what world does the agent grow up in."

r001.rationale: The response says environment design shapes model behavior during reinforcement learning, but it does not distinguish adapting an environment to a given model from proactively designing tools and environments while building a first-party product.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to design the tools and the environment together with the agent. You can’t just give a model a collection of APIs and assume it will know how to use them effectively. It needs to understand what actions are available, what those actions change, and how to tell whether it’s making progress.

For example, if an agent edits code, it should be able to run the code, inspect errors, and test its changes. That feedback loop is very important. Without it, the agent is mostly guessing. With it, it can try something, observe the result, and improve.

There’s also a balance in how much structure you provide. Very specialized tools can make a particular task easier, but they also constrain what the agent can do. More general tools give it flexibility, but require stronger reasoning. I would start with a small set of clear, composable tools and good feedback, then look at where the agent actually fails before adding more complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to design the tools and the environment together with the agent’s learning process. You can’t really separate them. What an agent can learn depends on what actions it can take, what feedback it receives, and whether it can tell if it has made progress.

For tools, I would start with a small set of clear, composable operations. Each tool should have a predictable interface and return useful feedback, including when something goes wrong. If a tool fails silently, the agent has very little basis for deciding what to do next. If it gets an informative error, it can potentially recover.

For environments, the important question is: can the agent try something, observe the consequences, and improve? You want tasks where success can be checked, but also enough variety that the agent has to learn a general strategy instead of memorizing a particular sequence of actions.

There’s a balance here. You want to remove unnecessary friction, but you don’t want to put all the intelligence into the tooling. Ideally, the tools provide reliable capabilities, and the agent learns how to combine them, check its work, and adapt when its first approach doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing tools and environments around an agent’s learning, but does not distinguish adapting an environment to a given model from proactively designing tools and environments for a first-party product.
